absent: Range arming path behavior beyond delegation, including queue insertion and reprogramming.
Callback time source and remaining-time sampling rules outside the shown helpers.
Clock base offset maintenance and clock-was-set propagation.
Timer queue ordering, timerqueue node layout, and expiry dispatch.
Numeric value of LOW_RES_NSEC and high resolution switching conditions.
Affinity applicator internals, notifier delivery, and mask allocation.
Soft interrupt dispatch order, tasklet queue linkage, and threaded interrupt flow.
Locking protocol for per-CPU base lock and sequence counter usage.

findings.text: Expiry adjustment advances a timer hard deadline together with its soft deadline by an identical offset so their separation stays constant. One helper uses a saturating time addition while the nanosecond helper uses plain integer addition.
Observers can read the stored hard deadline and separately the stored soft deadline. Remaining time is defined as hard deadline minus the time sampled for callbacks, using signed time subtraction.

For relative timers under low resolution builds the raw remaining interval is reduced by one global resolution quantum to cancel padding inserted at arm time. Absolute timers and other builds keep the raw difference unchanged.
Whether high resolution timers are active is either answered from a runtime patchable branch hint or answered constantly as inactive, depending on build configuration.
Timer granularity in the low resolution configuration is published as an unsigned value taken from LOW_RES_NSEC.
Timer instance carries a queue linkage member called node and also a pointer member called base toward its clock base. A boolean member called is_queued records queue membership.

The same instance carries boolean mode members named is_rel and additionally named is_soft and also named is_hard and finally named is_lazy. It also stores a soft timestamp named _softexpires and a callback named function that reports restart or not.

A clock base records its owning central base through member cpu_base and also its numeric position through member index and also its clock identity through member clockid. Ordering against concurrent updates uses a sequence counter named seq.

The same clock base tracks its next deadline in member expires_next and also its currently running timer in member running and also its pending queue in member active. A correction member called offset shifts clock readings.
Clock base kinds comprise four time domains called monotonic and realtime and boottime and tai, each present in a normal and a soft variant, followed by a count marker for the total number of bases.

Per CPU timer control starts with a raw spinlock member named lock and also a CPU number named cpu and also a bitmask of active bases named active_bases. A sequence member named clock_was_set_seq tracks clock changes.

The same control holds boolean state named hres_active and also named deferred_rearm and also named deferred_needs_update and also named hang_detected and also named softirq_activated and finally named online.

Expiry tracking keeps a hard deadline named expires_next with its timer named next_timer and also a soft deadline named softirq_expires_next with its timer named softirq_next_timer and also a deferred deadline named deferred_expires_next. Queued bases live in an array named clock_base sized by the maximum base count, with cross CPU signalling through member csd.

Optional high resolution diagnostics use member nr_events and also member nr_retries and also member nr_hangs and also member max_hang_time. Realtime builds add member softirq_expiry_lock and also member timer_waiters.

Arming with an explicit timeout delegates to a range arm with zero tolerance, while arming from stored expiries derives tolerance as hard minus soft converted to nanoseconds. A user variant reports whether the timer was already queued, using absolute or caller chosen timing modes.

Restart re-arms from stored expiries in absolute mode, forwarding advances a periodic timer from callback time by a caller interval, and a remaining query samples without adjusting for low resolution padding.
Queue membership is tested through a once read, and callback execution is detected by comparing the base running pointer against the queried timer.

Several helpers are intentional no-ops for restricted builds: dummy timeout always requests no restart, stack destruction does nothing, timer file clock notifications do nothing, cancel wait only relaxes the CPU, and CPU dying handling is a null pointer.
Time arithmetic treats timestamps as nanosecond integers, with addition of a count and subtraction of two stamps and conversion to nanoseconds all defined as plain integer operations.
Timer callbacks return one of two restart outcomes, where one value means do not requeue and the other means requeue the timer.

Deferred rearm uses a thread flag to remember pending work. Testing clears the flag under disabled interrupts and reports prior presence, while return to user logic consumes the flag and invokes rearm only when no scheduler reschedule request is also pending.
In builds without deferred rearm support all rearm helpers compile to empty operations that never report pending work.
Trigger none equals 0x00000000 and rising equals 0x00000001 and falling equals 0x00000002.
Trigger high equals 0x00000004 and low equals 0x00000008 and combined mask covers the four trigger bits and probe equals 0x00000010.
Flag shared equals 0x00000080 and probe-shared equals 0x00000100 and internal timer equals 0x00000200 and per-CPU equals 0x00000400.
Balancing control uses 0x00000800 and polling uses 0x00001000 and one-shot uses 0x00002000 and suspend exemption uses 0x00004000.
Forced resume uses 0x00008000 and thread prohibition uses 0x00010000 and early resume uses 0x00020000 and conditional suspend uses 0x00040000.

Automatic enable suppression uses 0x00080000 and debug suppression uses 0x00100000 and conditional one-shot uses 0x00200000. The public timer combination joins internal timer with suspend exemption and thread prohibition.
Interrupt context distinguishes hardirq from nested handling through two small enumerators, and handler functions take an integer line number plus a cookie pointer and return a disposition code.
Action descriptor stores a primary handler and also a device cookie that can be either shared or per-CPU and also an affinity mask and also a next pointer for sharing.

Same descriptor stores member thread_fn with member thread and also member secondary with member irq and also member flags with member thread_flags and also member thread_mask with member name and also member dir.
A high-bit marker at 1U shifted by 31 reports lines with no physical connection.
Affinity change notification carries a line number and also a reference count and also a work item and also a notify callback and also a release callback.
Affinity layout records pre vectors and also post vectors and also set count and also per-set sizes and also a set calculator and also private data.
Maximum affinity set count equals four.
Per-vector affinity description holds a CPU mask and a single-bit managed flag.

When affinity control exists, hint updates and combined affinity-plus-hint operations delegate to a common applicator with a flag distinguishing hint-only from enforced changes, and the legacy hint setter forwards to the combined form.

Without affinity support the setters report invalid argument, while force and capability and selection queries report neutral success or zero without acting, and descriptor updates also report invalid argument.
Notifier registration always reports success, mask creation always returns null, and vector calculation always returns the caller maximum.

Line disable pairs a non-synchronous disable with a conditional local CPU interrupt mask under lock validation builds, and enable reverses the order, with flag-saving variants preserving prior mask state.
Local CPU masking either emits tracing around raw mask operations or collapses to raw operations alone, depending on tracing configuration, covering plain disable and enable.
Flag-preserving save and restore similarly either add tracing based on prior mask state or collapse to raw save and restore alone.
Wake control enables or disables wake ability by forwarding a boolean to a common wake setter.
Chip state queries distinguish pending and active and masked and line-level conditions.
Threaded-handler forcing is either constantly true or governed by a runtime branch or constantly false across the three build variants.
Pending soft interrupt state lives in per-CPU storage, accessed by read and overwrite and read-modify-or helpers.
Soft interrupt numbers start with high-priority tasklets at zero followed by timer and network transmit and network receive and block handling in increasing order.
Later numbers continue with polling and tasklet and scheduler and high-resolution timer handling, ending with RCU as the required last entry before the total count.
Hotplug-safe soft interrupts comprise timer with polling with high-resolution timer with RCU.
Soft interrupt vector holds a single callback taking no arguments.

Timer soft interrupt accounting either reads a dedicated per-CPU counter under forced threading or falls back to the generic pending mask, raising goes through a timer thread when forced and through direct raise otherwise, and the current CPU softirq daemon task is fetched from per-CPU storage. A post-call flush helper simply invokes generic soft interrupt processing.

Tasklet descriptor links through member next and holds state in member state and disable depth in member count and a mode flag in member use_callback, with either a legacy function taking data or a modern callback taking the descriptor itself, plus a data word.

Declaration helpers create statically initialized tasklets in enabled or disabled form for both modern callback and legacy function styles, and a container helper recovers the enclosing structure from a callback pointer and field name.
Tasklet lifetime uses a scheduled bit meaning queued for execution and a run bit meaning currently executing on another CPU.

Multiprocessor builds acquire execution with an atomic test-and-set on the run bit and provide blocking and spinning waits for unlock, while single-processor builds treat locking as always successful with empty unlock operations.
Normal and high-priority scheduling each set the scheduled bit atomically and enqueue only when the bit was previously clear.

Disabling increments the count with ordering against later checks, enabling decrements with prior ordering, and atomic-context or process-context disable additionally waits for any running instance before a full barrier.
Queue flag reads use a once accessor paired with queue update paths, deferred rearm testing requires interrupts disabled, and timer raising asserts interrupt context.
Tasklet disable relies on atomic count plus explicit barriers and unlock waits; omitting the wait or barrier could let a running instance overlap with teardown.

Header guards protect each timer and interrupt header from multiple inclusion, clock-base alignment expands to cacheline alignment or to nothing by build, and the generic hard-disable helper expands to an empty loop.
